title: Bartholomew Bumble's Button Blunder
markdown:
Life along Narrowboat Lane was a peculiar, peaceful business. Boats of every stripe bobbed at their moorings, each a little painted house, and the air kept a faint census of canal water and woodsmoke. Among those floating gardens lived Bartholomew Bumble, a goat of uncommon determination and an even more uncommon hobby. He was a gardener first. His prize petunias, velvety and sunset-coloured, could make a neighbour stop mid-towpath and forget what they had come to say.

He also kept a notebook. Not a diary. A leather-bound book of suspiciously small mysteries. Bartholomew had an eye for the curious: the disappearing handle from Mrs. Gable's favourite teacup, the sock that never came home on Tuesdays from young Timmy's line, the perfectly circular puddle that vanished after a sunny hour as if it had an appointment elsewhere. He sketched diagrams with a stubby pencil held in his hoof, brow furrowed, whiskers serious as a magistrate's.

His best friend Otis, a tortoise of immense patience, often found him muttering at the canal's edge. Otis moved at his own unhurried pace. His shell took the sun as if it had been polished for the occasion, and his advice was always worth the wait.

"And wouldn't you know it, Otis," Bartholomew would say, pointing at a smudge on a mossy stone, "that's the third time this week I've found a lone, perfectly round pebble just here. Smooth as a marble. A sign? A marker?"

Otis, usually occupied with a succulent dandelion, would offer a slow blink. "Perhaps," he would rumble, voice like pebbles shifting in a stream, "it signifies a pebble. A very round pebble, indeed."

Bartholomew would sigh, goat-breath in a little cloud, and then his eyes would catch the next riddle. Today it was the missing button from Mrs. Higgins's favourite gardening apron: polished horn, much loved. He had been sketching a faint scuff near her rusty watering can when, in his enthusiastic lean, his elbow found his prize Sunset Blush pot.

The terracotta tipped. It struck the narrowboat's planks. Soil and pink petals flew, some of them choosing the canal. Bartholomew's heart skipped like a stone thrown too hard. Lunch was in an hour. Mrs. Higgins would see the wreck. He had to hide it. Quick.

His mind, usually so sharp for vanished buttons, spun. He spotted driftwood on the towpath and a bit of charcoal from his sketching kit. He would make a sign. Something official. In his most determined goat-hand he wrote: PLEASE NOTE: Temporary Petunia Relocation Due to Urgent Botanical Research. Back Soon. Signed, B. Bumble, Chief Botanist.

He propped the sign near the ruin and scooped soil into the cracked pot, muttering apologies to the blooms. A petal stuck to his hoof. He shook it off as if it were evidence. He was still dusting himself when Mr. Abernathy, the canal captain, came polishing brass on the next boat, beard like a well-kept hedge.

"Morning, Bartholomew." The captain squinted at the sign. "Urgent botanical research, you say? Is that why all these little things have been appearing around the boats?" He pointed to a neat pile of bottle caps on his own deck, then to a nest of colourful buttons on the pontoon.

Bartholomew's ears drooped. "Things?"

"Yes, things," chirped Lily from the boat next door, pigtails bouncing. She held up a spool of green thread. "I thought it was treasure for my dolly's dress."

A small chorus followed. Old Mr. Henderson had a shiny coin. Little Daisy had a skipping stone worn smooth by a hundred pockets. Even grumpy Mr. Fitzwilliam showed a painted wooden bird from his doorstep. They were all artfully arranged, Bartholomew saw, in the very places where he had stood with his notebook, mind miles away in deduction. He had not been leaving clues for himself. He had been making little hoards while he thought.

He looked at the notebook. He looked at the wobbling sign. He looked at the kind, puzzled faces. His stomach performed a small, unhappy flip.

"Oh dear," he mumbled. "I might have made a mistake. A rather large one."

Otis, who had arrived at last, nudged Bartholomew's hoof with a leathery nose. "Bartholomew. The most useful research is often about the mess in front of you."

The lane waited. Water ticked against the hulls. Bartholomew took down the sign. He folded it once, as if folding might make the official nonsense smaller, and held the driftwood as what it was: a stick with a fib on it.

"I'm very sorry," he said, voice finding its feet. "I was trying to solve Mrs. Higgins's missing button. When I concentrate, I move things. And then I knocked over her petunias, and I wrote that notice instead of saying so."

Quiet again. Then Mrs. Higgins herself, flour on her apron as if it were a permanent decoration, chuckled.

"You silly goat. Urgent research? Why didn't you just say you'd had a little accident?" She surveyed the scattered petunias. "A few petals won't hurt. We can replant them. And perhaps you could use that excellent eye to help me find a few more buttons. I seem to be losing them left, right, and centre."

Relief arrived, warmer than the panic had been. The air smelled of wet earth and someone else's stew.

"As for the button mystery," Mr. Abernathy said, stroking his chin, "the other day I saw a magpie leaving your boat with something peculiar in its beak. Looked rather like a shiny button to me."

The shiny things, the colourful things, the smooth things: not clues. A magpie's shopping. Bartholomew's urgent botanical research had only been a goat covering a crash. The real mystery was simpler, and funnier, than any diagram in the leather book.

He opened the notebook to a clean page. He did not write a lecture. He wrote a heading, small and honest: Mysteries Solved by Magpies (and Goat-Related Oopsies). Then he set the broken pot upright, pressed soil around the remaining stems, and left the folded sign under a stone where only Otis would see it. A magpie clicked from the tiller, considering the afternoon as if the afternoon were a bead. Bartholomew put his stubby pencil away. The petunias, slightly fewer, still held their sunset.
characters: Bartholomew Bumble (determined goat gardener), Otis (tortoise friend), Mrs. Higgins (kind canal neighbour)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing story for older children
